## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

1	# Repository templates — the catalog
2	
3	> DevDesk architecture notes. Referenced from `.claude/CLAUDE.md`;
4	> read this file when working on the code it describes.
5	
6	`internal/template` is the catalog of templates a new repository can be filled
7	from, and how their files are fetched. `internal/ui/templates` is the
8	`:templates` view over it (below). The picker in the creation form comes later;
9	the plan is `.claude/plans/2026-09-18-repo-templates.md`.
10	
11	## An entry is a reference
12	
13	An `Entry` holds a slug, a name, a description, tags and a `Source`. The content
14	stays where it is and is fetched when a repository is created from it, so a
15	template cannot drift from its original.
16	
17	| `Source.Kind` | `URL` | `Path` | `Ref` |
18	|---|---|---|---|
19	| `git` | clone URL | optional subdirectory, made the root | branch, tag or SHA |
20	| `local` | — | repository directory | branch, tag or SHA |
21	| `oci` | registry URL | repository | tag |
22	
23	The catalog is **global**: `~/.devdesk/templates.yaml`, not one per context.
24	Every entry is declared. There used to be a second source, entries listed from a
25	registry's `/v2/_catalog` and merged in; it was removed because nobody used it,
26	and an OCI template is declared by hand like any other. `registry.templates_repository`
27	is therefore read by nothing and stays in the schema only so existing files
28	still load.
29	
30	## Fetching
31	
32	`Fetch(ctx, src, Credentials)` returns `[]File{Path, Content []byte, Executable}`.
33	
34	- **git and local both go through `git archive`.** What comes back is what was
35	  *committed*: no `.git`, nothing ignored, no uncommitted edit — a template must
36	  not depend on someone's working tree. A directory that is not a repository is
37	  refused, not copied raw. `.gitattributes export-ignore` is honoured, which is
38	  git's own answer to "what is part of a release".
39	- **git remote** is `init` + `fetch --depth 1 <ref>` + `archive FETCH_HEAD`, in a
40	  temp directory removed before returning. `clone --branch` would refuse a SHA,
41	  and a template pinned to a SHA is the reproducible kind. Nothing is cached yet:
42	  `F` (sync) in the view is what will own a cache.
43	- **oci** reuses `oci.Client.DownloadTemplate`, which returns `Entries`
44	  (bytes + execute bit).
45	- A symlink in a template is **refused**, naming it and saying to replace it
46	  with a regular file. It used to be read as an empty file — a template silently
47	  missing what it says it holds. A **submodule** is refused the same way
48	  (`git ls-tree` finds the gitlink): `git archive` writes it as an empty
49	  directory, which would be the same silent gap.
50	
51	**Credentials are resolved per host** by `CredentialsFor(cfg, secrets, src)`: the
52	forge's token goes only to a git source on the forge's host, the registry's
53	password only to an OCI source on the registry's, and anything else is fetched
54	anonymously — a token authenticates one host, and the catalog can be shared, so
55	the entry cannot be what decides. Nothing is sent over `http://` either, even to
56	the forge's own host. A private repository on any other host is not
57	reachable over HTTPS: use an SSH URL. Both the view and the explorer call it, so
58	the rule has one place to live.
59	
60	**A template has limits: 500 files and 32 MiB** (`MaxFiles`, `MaxBytes`),
61	checked inside `Fetch` and so before anything is created on the forge. They are
62	enforced **while reading**, not after: `git archive`'s output is capped
63	(`git.ErrOutputTooLarge`) and the tar/gzip readers stop at the limits
64	(`oci.Limits`, `oci.ErrArchiveTooLarge`), so a huge repository or a gzip bomb
65	is never held in memory whole. `checkLimits` still names the biggest file for
66	what got that far. GitLab
67	takes every file in one request, so the body size decides; GitHub takes one
68	request per file, one after the other, so the count does. The numbers are
69	estimates: the one to verify against a real GitLab instance is its maximum
70	request body, which has to admit 32 MiB once base64-encoded (about 43 MiB).
71	
72	## The catalog file is not trusted
73	
74	It can be shared or hand-edited, so `Entry.Validate` runs on `Put` **and on
75	load**. A bad entry, or a slug declared twice, does not fail `Open`: it is set
76	aside (`Store.Problems()`, reported as a footer warning), the rest of the
77	catalog stays usable, and the entry stays in the file so saving another one
78	does not delete a hand-edited line:
79	
80	- git URLs must be `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git` or scp-form. `ext::` runs a
81	  command and `file://` reads this machine; a checkout on this machine is the
82	  `local` kind precisely so neither is needed.
83	- A URL or ref beginning with `-` is refused — git would read it as an option.
84	  `internal/git` repeats that check, since it is the last stop before `exec`.
85	
86	Writes go to a sibling file renamed over the catalog, and memory only changes if
87	the write succeeded, so a failure leaves both agreeing.
88	
89	## The `:templates` view — `internal/ui/templates`
90	
91	A `datatable` (icon, Name, Tags, Source, Ref) over the catalog. The body is
92	always the table (Rule 139); the count is in the header.
93	
94	| Key | Does |
95	|---|---|
96	| `N` | new entry — form in the viewport (Rule 112), source kind is a `←→` cycle field (Rule 132) |
97	| `E` | edit |
98	| `D` | delete after a confirmation that defaults to No |
99	| `S` | scan the template for vulnerabilities and secrets (below) |
100	| `V` | preview: asks the router to open the viewer on a listing of the files the template would put in a repository (`previewSource`), so a fetch failure is reported by the viewer's own load path |
101	| `.` `/` | sort, filter (name, description, tags, source) |
102	
103	**The slug is derived from the name on creation and fixed on edit.** Renaming a
104	template must not orphan whatever remembered its old slug.
105	
106	**A local source has no URL field**; the same three inputs (`url`, `path`,
107	`ref`) serve every kind and only their labels change, so a value typed before
108	cycling the kind is kept.
109	
110	**An unreadable catalog refuses every write.** Saving over a file that could
111	not be parsed would replace whatever the user had in it; the footer says so and
112	`N`/`E`/`D` are greyed with the reason. The catalog not being *open yet* is not
113	greyed — that is not knowing, and greying it for one read would look like a
114	glitch (Rule 130).
115	
116	## Creating a repository from a template
117	
118	The `Template` field of the explorer's creation form (projects only) shows
119	`none` — an empty repository — until one is chosen.
120	
121	- **`enter` on the field opens the catalog**, lent by the router in selection
122	  mode (`templates.NewForSelection`), the second borrow the explorer makes (see
123	  `scanning.md`). The form is kept as it is meanwhile; `enter` in the picker
124	  answers `TemplateSelectedMsg{Slug, Name}`, `esc` answers
125	  `SelectionCancelledMsg`, and the router turns them into the explorer's own
126	  `TemplateChosenMsg` / `TemplateChoiceCancelledMsg`. `backspace` on the field
127	  puts it back to none.
128	- **The picker is the whole catalog**, filterable and sortable, with `V` to look
129	  inside. N, E and D are not bound there — a mode replaces the list (Rule 130).
130	  The form keeps the slug and shows the name; the slug is what is submitted.
131	- **The template is fetched before the repository is created.** A bad ref, a
132	  network failure, a refused login, a template that is gone from the catalog or
133	  one over the limits all fail with *nothing created*: the footer says so and the
134	  run detail reads `template unavailable — nothing was created`. Only the initial
135	  commit can still fail once the repository exists, and that keeps the old
136	  outcome: the repository stays, empty, and the footer says it was created empty.
137	  The run item is **failed** (`created empty — the template's commit failed`), not
138	  done: what was asked for was a repository with a template in it.
139	- **A create is bounded, not cancellable.** `jobs.Kind.Cancellable` says no for
140	  `create` (a request already sent cannot be un-sent), so the guard against a
141	  stalled forge is a timeout: one minute for the repository, ten for the initial
142	  commit (GitHub makes one request per file).
143	- The catalog is read when the template is applied, not when the form opens, so
144	  a template deleted while the form was open is reported as no longer in the
145	  catalog rather than applied from a stale copy.
146	
147	## Scanning a template
148	
149	A secret in a template ends up in every repository made from it, so `S` scans
150	what the template would put in a repository — before it does.
151	
152	The template is fetched, written to **`~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>`**
153	(`template.Materialize`, which replaces whatever a previous scan left there), and
154	that directory is scanned as a plain directory by the configured scanners. It is
155	reused as a directory scan on purpose: the result is cached by path
156	(`cache.StoreWorkspaceScan`, now shared with the workspaces view), so it appears
157	in the **`:sec` inventory** and opens in the same results view, with nothing new
158	to build. The footer here says how it ended — the counts, or `no findings`, or a
159	warning when a stage failed and found nothing (which is not the same claim). The
160	workspaces list is not involved: the copy is not in it, and nothing pretends it is.
161	
162	- **Fixed directory, not a temp one**, because the scan is cached by path: a
163	  fresh directory per scan would leave a dead `:sec` entry behind for each.
164	- **`Materialize` computes and empties only its own directory.** It takes a slug,
165	  validates it, and derives the path — a caller cannot point the removal
166	  elsewhere — and refuses a file whose path would land outside it.
167	- **No CI score.** A template has no pipeline to grade, and plumber would look
168	  for a remote it does not have.
169	- **It is registry work** (`jobs.KindScan`, origin `:templates`), so `:jobs`
170	  lists it, `K` stops it, and the router stamps the context the counts are stored
171	  under (D68). `ScanStartingMsg` and `ScanCompleteMsg` implement `jobs.Reporter`
172	  and are routed through `routeWork`; a test pins that, because implementing the
173	  interface proves nothing if the router never calls it.
174	- **`S` is greyed** when neither Trivy nor Gitleaks is available, and while a
175	  scan of that template is running (whoever started it). Until the scanner check
176	  comes back it stays lit — greying it for a few frames would read as a glitch
177	  (Rule 130). The picker has no `S`.
178	
179	## Not done yet
180	
181	- `F` (sync) and the cache it would own: every preview, creation and scan
182	  refetches.
183	- A private git repository on a host that is not the forge's is fetched
184	  anonymously, so it fails with git's own reason: use an SSH URL.
185	- No spinner on the row itself: the footer status carries the live scan.

forge's token goes only to a git source on the forge's host, the registry's
password only to an OCI source on the registry's, and anything else is fetched
anonymously — a token authenticates one host, and the catalog can be shared, so
the entry cannot be what decides. Nothing is sent over `http://` either, even to
the forge's own host. A private repository on any other host is not
reachable over HTTPS: use an SSH URL. Both the view and the explorer call it, so
the rule has one place to live.

**A template has limits: 500 files and 32 MiB** (`MaxFiles`, `MaxBytes`),
checked inside `Fetch` and so before anything is created on the forge. They are
enforced **while reading**, not after: `git archive`'s output is capped
(`git.ErrOutputTooLarge`) and the tar/gzip readers stop at the limits
(`oci.Limits`, `oci.ErrArchiveTooLarge`), so a huge repository or a gzip bomb
is never held in memory whole. `checkLimits` still names the biggest file for
what got that far. GitLab
takes every file in one request, so the body size decides; GitHub takes one
request per file, one after the other, so the count does. The numbers are
estimates: the one to verify against a real GitLab instance is its maximum
request body, which has to admit 32 MiB once base64-encoded (about 43 MiB).

## The catalog file is not trusted

It can be shared or hand-edited, so `Entry.Validate` runs on `Put` **and on
load**. A bad entry, or a slug declared twice, does not fail `Open`: it is set
aside (`Store.Problems()`, reported as a footer warning), the rest of the
catalog stays usable, and the entry stays in the file so saving another one
does not delete a hand-edited line:

- git URLs must be `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git` or scp-form. `ext::` runs a
  command and `file://` reads this machine; a checkout on this machine is the
  `local` kind precisely so neither is needed.
- A URL or ref beginning with `-` is refused — git would read it as an option.
  `internal/git` repeats that check, since it is the last stop before `exec`.

Writes go to a sibling file renamed over the catalog, and memory only changes if
the write succeeded, so a failure leaves both agreeing.

## The `:templates` view — `internal/ui/templates`

A `datatable` (icon, Name, Tags, Source, Ref) over the catalog. The body is
always the table (Rule 139); the count is in the header.

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `N` | new entry — form in the viewport (Rule 112), source kind is a `←→` cycle field (Rule 132) |
| `E` | edit |
| `D` | delete after a confirmation that defaults to No |
| `S` | scan the template for vulnerabilities and secrets (below) |
| `V` | preview: asks the router to open the viewer on a listing of the files the template would put in a repository (`previewSource`), so a fetch failure is reported by the viewer's own load path |
| `.` `/` | sort, filter (name, description, tags, source) |

**The slug is derived from the name on creation and fixed on edit.** Renaming a
template must not orphan whatever remembered its old slug.

**A local source has no URL field**; the same three inputs (`url`, `path`,
`ref`) serve every kind and only their labels change, so a value typed before
cycling the kind is kept.

**An unreadable catalog refuses every write.** Saving over a file that could
not be parsed would replace whatever the user had in it; the footer says so and
`N`/`E`/`D` are greyed with the reason. The catalog not being *open yet* is not
greyed — that is not knowing, and greying it for one read would look like a
glitch (Rule 130).

## Creating a repository from a template

The `Template` field of the explorer's creation form (projects only) shows
`none` — an empty repository — until one is chosen.

- **`enter` on the field opens the catalog**, lent by the router in selection
  mode (`templates.NewForSelection`), the second borrow the explorer makes (see
  `scanning.md`). The form is kept as it is meanwhile; `enter` in the picker
  answers `TemplateSelectedMsg{Slug, Name}`, `esc` answers
  `SelectionCancelledMsg`, and the router turns them into the explorer's own
  `TemplateChosenMsg` / `TemplateChoiceCancelledMsg`. `backspace` on the field
  puts it back to none.
- **The picker is the whole catalog**, filterable and sortable, with `V` to look
  inside. N, E and D are not bound there — a mode replaces the list (Rule 130).
  The form keeps the slug and shows the name; the slug is what is submitted.
- **The template is fetched before the repository is created.** A bad ref, a
  network failure, a refused login, a template that is gone from the catalog or
  one over the limits all fail with *nothing created*: the footer says so and the
  run detail reads `template unavailable — nothing was created`. Only the initial
  commit can still fail once the repository exists, and that keeps the old
  outcome: the repository stays, empty, and the footer says it was created empty.
  The run item is **failed** (`created empty — the template's commit failed`), not
  done: what was asked for was a repository with a template in it.
- **A create is bounded, not cancellable.** `jobs.Kind.Cancellable` says no for
  `create` (a request already sent cannot be un-sent), so the guard against a
  stalled forge is a timeout: one minute for the repository, ten for the initial
  commit (GitHub makes one request per file).
- The catalog is read when the template is applied, not when the form opens, so
  a template deleted while the form was open is reported as no longer in the
  catalog rather than applied from a stale copy.

## Scanning a template

A secret in a template ends up in every repository made from it, so `S` scans
what the template would put in a repository — before it does.

The template is fetched, written to **`~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>`**
(`template.Materialize`, which replaces whatever a previous scan left there), and
that directory is scanned as a plain directory by the configured scanners. It is
reused as a directory scan on purpose: the result is cached by path
(`cache.StoreWorkspaceScan`, now shared with the workspaces view), so it appears
in the **`:sec` inventory** and opens in the same results view, with nothing new
to build. The footer here says how it ended — the counts, or `no findings`, or a
warning when a stage failed and found nothing (which is not the same claim). The
workspaces list is not involved: the copy is not in it, and nothing pretends it is.

- **Fixed directory, not a temp one**, because the scan is cached by path: a
  fresh directory per scan would leave a dead `:sec` entry behind for each.
- **`Materialize` computes and empties only its own directory.** It takes a slug,
  validates it, and derives the path — a caller cannot point the removal
  elsewhere — and refuses a file whose path would land outside it.
- **No CI score.** A template has no pipeline to grade, and plumber would look
  for a remote it does not have.
- **It is registry work** (`jobs.KindScan`, origin `:templates`), so `:jobs`
  lists it, `K` stops it, and the router stamps the context the counts are stored
  under (D68). `ScanStartingMsg` and `ScanCompleteMsg` implement `jobs.Reporter`
  and are routed through `routeWork`; a test pins that, because implementing the
  interface proves nothing if the router never calls it.
- **`S` is greyed** when neither Trivy nor Gitleaks is available, and while a
  scan of that template is running (whoever started it). Until the scanner check
  comes back it stays lit — greying it for a few frames would read as a glitch
  (Rule 130). The picker has no `S`.

## Not done yet

- `F` (sync) and the cache it would own: every preview, creation and scan
  refetches.
- A private git repository on a host that is not the forge's is fetched
  anonymously, so it fails with git's own reason: use an SSH URL.
- No spinner on the row itself: the footer status carries the live scan.

Deux approches possibles, et le choix dépend d'un point technique que DevDesk tranche déjà pour toi.

**Option recommandée — un seul repo git, plusieurs entrées `git` avec des `Path` différents**

Dans `~/.devdesk/templates.yaml`, une entrée par template :
```yaml
- slug: go-http-api
  source: {kind: git, url: git@github.com:toi/templates.git, path: go/http-api, ref: v1.2.0}
- slug: node-express
  source: {kind: git, url: git@github.com:toi/templates.git, path: node/express, ref: v1.2.0}
```
Même repo, même URL, `path` = le sous-dossier de l'arborescence langage/framework, `ref` = un tag figé (pas `main`, sinon un template change sous les repos déjà créés avec).

Pas besoin de clone local : DevDesk fait un `git init` + `fetch --depth 1 <ref>` + `archive` à chaque usage (`internal/template/fetch.go:100`). Ça ne prend que ce qui est **committé** — pas de `.git`, pas de fichiers ignorés, pas de modifs non commitées, symlinks et submodules refusés explicitement. Pas encore de cache (le sync `F` est prévu mais pas fait), donc chaque preview/scan/création refetch.

**Ton idée — clone local + référence sur disque (`kind: local`)**

Ça existe (`Source.Kind: local`, `Path` = répertoire du repo), mais **actuellement ça ne prend pas de sous-dossier** — `fetch.go:107` appelle `git.ArchiveLocal` avec un sous-chemin vide en dur, contrairement au `kind: git` distant qui, lui, accepte un `Path`. Donc avec une seule arborescence multi-langages clonée une fois, chaque entrée `local` récupérerait **tout le repo**, pas le sous-dossier voulu.

Pour que ton schéma marche avec `local`, il faudrait soit :
- cloner un checkout séparé par langage/framework (perd l'intérêt du repo unique), soit
- étendre `KindLocal` pour accepter un `Path` de sous-dossier comme `KindGit` (petit changement dans `internal/template/fetch.go` + `template.go` + le formulaire `:templates`).

Sauf besoin de travailler hors-ligne, je partirais sur la première option : un seul repo distant, une entrée par sous-dossier, tags pour figer les versions.

17		Description string `json:"Description"`
18		StartLine   int    `json:"StartLine"`
19		EndLine     int    `json:"EndLine"`

27		Author      string `json:"Author,omitempty"`
28		Email       string `json:"Email,omitempty"`

33	// gitleaksSecretsFound is the exit code Gitleaks uses to say it found
34	// something. It is a result, not a failure — but it is not only that: gitleaks
35	// exits 1 for a fatal error too, and what separates them is the report. See
36	// RunGitleaks.
37	const gitleaksSecretsFound = 1
38	
39	// gitleaksConfigMount is where a configured rules file is mounted inside the
40	// container, so the argument passed to gitleaks is never the host path.
41	//
42	// The container root is where it goes because that is the one place nothing
43	// else can be: the scanned target is mounted at containerScanPath, so no file
44	// of the repository can land beside it, and the image itself holds no
45	// /gitleaks.toml — its root is a plain Alpine tree (checked on
46	// zricethezav/gitleaks v8.30.1). Writing the name down here is the point: a
47	// mount path chosen at the call site is one nobody can check against the
48	// target's.
49	const gitleaksConfigMount = "/gitleaks.toml"
50	
51	// gitleaksArgs builds the invocation. Gitleaks writes its report to a path
52	// rather than to stdout, so the report path is redirected at the process's own
53	// stdout — which is a different pseudo-file inside a container.
54	func gitleaksArgs(target string, tool ToolSpec, history bool, configPath string) toolCmd {
55		docker := tool.Source == ToolSourceContainer
56	
57		// In Docker mode the flag has to name the mount rather than the host path.
58		// The file is not in the container otherwise, and gitleaks then dies before
59		// scanning anything — which used to be reported as a clean repository (D56).
60		flagPath := configPath
61		if docker && configPath != "" {
62			flagPath = gitleaksConfigMount
63		}
64	
65		appendOptions := func(args []string) []string {
66			// History is the expensive mode, so it is opted into by dropping
67			// --no-git rather than by adding a flag.
68			if !history {
69				args = append(args, "--no-git")
70			}
71			if configPath != "" {
72				args = append(args, "--config", flagPath)
73			}
74			return args
75		}
76	
77		if docker {
78			image := gitleaksImage(tool.Image)
79			args := []string{
80				"run", "--rm",
81				"-v", target + ":" + containerScanPath + ":ro",
82			}
83			// Before the image name: everything after it is gitleaks' own argv.
84			if configPath != "" {
85				args = append(args, "-v", configPath+":"+gitleaksConfigMount+":ro")
86			}
87			args = append(args,
88				image,
89				"detect",
90				"--source", containerScanPath,
91				"--gitleaks-ignore-path", containerScanPath,
92				"--report-format", "json",
93				"--report-path", "/dev/fd/1",
94			)
95			return toolCmd{Name: engine.Current().Binary, Args: appendOptions(args)}
96		}
97	
98		args := []string{
99			"detect",
100			"--source", target,
101			"--gitleaks-ignore-path", target,
102			"--report-format", "json",
103			"--report-path", "/dev/stdout",
104		}
105		return toolCmd{Name: gitleaksBinary(tool), Args: appendOptions(args)}
106	}
107	
108	// checkGitleaksConfig refuses a rules file that cannot be read, before
109	// anything is started.
110	//
111	// It is not the guard against a bad configuration — RunGitleaks is, and it
112	// reports gitleaks' own diagnostic, which also covers a file that exists and
113	// does not parse. This one exists for the side effect: `docker run -v` on a
114	// host path that is not there does not fail, it **creates a directory** at that
115	// path and mounts it (measured on Docker Desktop 29.7.2, which made a
116	// `nope.toml/` and its parent). A typo in gitleaks_config would leave
117	// directories on the user's disk, once per scan.
118	func checkGitleaksConfig(path string) error {
119		if path == "" {
120			return nil
121		}
122		f, err := os.Open(path) //nolint:gosec // the path is the user's own setting
123		if err != nil {
124			return fmt.Errorf("gitleaks config: %w", err)
125		}
126		return f.Close()
127	}
128	
129	// RunGitleaks executes Gitleaks and returns findings.
130	// progressFn is an optional callback called with each stderr line.
131	//
132	// Gitleaks exits 1 for two unrelated things, and telling them apart is the
133	// whole of D56. Measured on v8.30.1:
134	//
135	//	clean          exit 0, stdout "[]"
136	//	secrets found  exit 1, stdout the report
137	//	fatal error    exit 1, stdout empty
138	//
139	// So the report is what separates a result from a failure, and an exit 1 with
140	// nothing on stdout is **never** a clean repository. It used to be read as one:
141	// a --config gitleaks could not load died before scanning a single byte, and
142	// the scan came back with SecretsScanned true and no findings — a green icon in
143	// ws for a repository nobody had looked at.
144	func RunGitleaks(ctx context.Context, target string, tool ToolSpec, history bool, configPath string, progressFn func(string)) ([]Finding, error) {
145		if err := checkGitleaksConfig(configPath); err != nil {
146			return nil, err
147		}
148	
149		stdout, err := runner.Run(ctx, gitleaksArgs(target, tool, history, configPath), progressFn)
150		if err != nil {
151			// A report alongside exit 1 is gitleaks saying it found something.
152			// Anything else — another exit code, a process that never ran, or an
153			// exit 1 with no report at all — is a failure, and carries gitleaks'
154			// own stderr with it.
155			var exit *exitError
156			if len(stdout) == 0 || !errors.As(err, &exit) || exit.Code != gitleaksSecretsFound {
157				return nil, fmt.Errorf("gitleaks failed: %w", err)
158			}
159		}
160	
161		if len(stdout) == 0 {
162			return []Finding{}, nil
163		}
164		return parseGitleaksOutput(stdout)
165	}
166	
167	// parseGitleaksOutput parses Gitleaks JSON output into findings
168	func parseGitleaksOutput(data []byte) ([]Finding, error) {
169		var gitleaksFindings []GitleaksFinding
170		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &gitleaksFindings); err != nil {
171			return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to parse gitleaks output: %w", err)
172		}
173	
174		findings := make([]Finding, 0, len(gitleaksFindings))
175	
176		for _, gf := range gitleaksFindings {
177			findings = append(findings, Finding{
178				ID:          gf.RuleID,
179				Title:       fmt.Sprintf("Secret detected: %s", gf.RuleID),
180				Description: gf.Description,
181				Severity:    SeverityHigh, // Secrets are always high severity
182				Source:      "gitleaks",
183				File:        gf.File,
184				Line:        gf.StartLine,
185				Match:       maskSecret(gf.Secret),
186				Fingerprint: gf.Fingerprint,
187			})
188		}
189	
190		return findings, nil
191	}
192	
193	// GetGitleaksCommand returns the command that would be executed, for display
194	// and logging. It is built by the same builder as the executed command, so the
195	// two cannot drift apart.
196	func GetGitleaksCommand(target string, tool ToolSpec, history bool, configPath string) string {
197		return gitleaksArgs(target, tool, history, configPath).String()
198	}

200	// AddToGitleaksIgnore adds a finding to the .gitleaksignore file in the target directory
201	// Returns nil if already present (silently skips duplicates)
202	func AddToGitleaksIgnore(targetDir string, finding Finding) (err error) {
203		ignorePath := targetDir + "/.gitleaksignore"
204	
205		// Use the fingerprint as the ignore entry (gitleaks native format)
206		entry := finding.Fingerprint
207		if entry == "" {
208			// Fallback: build fingerprint manually
209			entry = fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%d", finding.File, finding.ID, finding.Line)
210		}
211	
212		// Check if entry already exists
213		if existingContent, readErr := os.ReadFile(ignorePath); readErr == nil {
214			if strings.Contains(string(existingContent), entry) {
215				// Already present, silently skip
216				return nil
217			}
218		}
219	
220		// Open file in append mode, create if doesn't exist
221		f, err := os.OpenFile(ignorePath, os.O_APPEND|os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY, 0644)
222		if err != nil {
223			return fmt.Errorf("failed to open .gitleaksignore: %w", err)
224		}
225		defer func() {
226			if cerr := f.Close(); cerr != nil && err == nil {
227				err = fmt.Errorf("failed to close .gitleaksignore: %w", cerr)
228			}
229		}()
230	
231		if _, err := f.WriteString(entry + "\n"); err != nil {
232			return fmt.Errorf("failed to write to .gitleaksignore: %w", err)
233		}
234	
235		return nil
236	}

1	package scan
2	
3	import (
4		"bufio"
5		"bytes"
6		"context"
7		"errors"
8		"fmt"
9		"os/exec"
10		"strings"
11	)
12	
13	// toolCmd is one subprocess invocation: the binary and the arguments handed to
14	// it. Building it is pure, which is what makes the argument surface — the part
15	// that decides what a scanner is actually asked to do — testable without a
16	// scanner installed.
17	//
18	// It is also what the UI displays. Deriving the shown command and the executed
19	// one from the same value is the point: the two used to be built separately and
20	// had drifted (§1.3 D19).
21	type toolCmd struct {
22		Name string
23		Args []string
24		// Env is the child's whole environment when it is not nil, os.Environ()
25		// plus what the caller added. It exists so a credential can reach a tool
26		// without going through argv, which is readable from the process list —
27		// the arrangement the clone already uses for http.extraHeader (§3.16).
28		//
29		// String() never renders it: the invocation is logged and shown in the UI.
30		Env []string
31	
32		// Dir is the working directory the tool runs in, when it has one.
33		//
34		// It exists for plumber, whose `analyze` takes **no path argument**: it
35		// works on the current directory. Without this the tool ran in whatever
36		// directory DevDesk was launched from and reported
37		// `--project is required (could not auto-detect from git remote)` — a
38		// failure about a repository nobody had asked it to look at. Trivy and
39		// Gitleaks take their target in argv and set nothing here.
40		Dir string
41	}
42	
43	// String renders the invocation as a shell command line, for logs and for the
44	// command the UI shows next to a scan.
45	func (c toolCmd) String() string {
46		if c.Name == "" {
47			return ""
48		}
49		line := strings.Join(append([]string{c.Name}, c.Args...), " ")
50		// The directory is part of what the command means when the tool takes no
51		// path: a logged invocation that cannot be re-run says less than it looks
52		// like it does.
53		if c.Dir != "" {
54			return "cd " + c.Dir + " && " + line
55		}
56		return line
57	}
58	
59	// exitError reports a tool that ran and exited non-zero. The code matters:
60	// both scanners use a non-zero exit to mean "I found something" rather than
61	// "I failed" — trivy for vulnerabilities, gitleaks for secrets — so callers
62	// have to tell the two apart.
63	type exitError struct {
64		Code   int
65		Stderr string
66	}
67	
68	func (e *exitError) Error() string {
69		if e.Stderr != "" {
70			return fmt.Sprintf("exit status %d: %s", e.Code, strings.TrimSpace(e.Stderr))
71		}
72		return fmt.Sprintf("exit status %d", e.Code)
73	}
74	
75	// commandRunner is the seam every subprocess in this package passes through.
76	//
77	// The package drives trivy and gitleaks as external processes, which makes it
78	// untestable without both installed and a repository to point them at. Routing
79	// through this interface lets tests exercise the argument building, the
80	// exit-code handling and the output parsing — where the defects live — against
81	// canned output.
82	type commandRunner interface {
83		// Run executes tc and returns what it wrote to stdout. Lines written to
84		// stderr are forwarded to progressFn as they arrive, which is how Trivy
85		// reports its database download. A tool that runs and exits non-zero
86		// returns its stdout along with an *exitError.
87		Run(ctx context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]byte, error)
88	}
89	
90	// cliRunner is the production commandRunner: it shells out to the real tools.
91	type cliRunner struct{}
92	
93	func (cliRunner) Run(ctx context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]byte, error) {
94		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, tc.Name, tc.Args...) //nolint:gosec // name is one of trivy/gitleaks/plumber/docker
95		cmd.Env = tc.Env                                     // nil inherits this process's environment, which is the default
96		cmd.Dir = tc.Dir                                     // empty runs in DevDesk's own working directory
97	
98		var stdout bytes.Buffer
99		cmd.Stdout = &stdout
100	
101		// Stderr is consumed two ways: streamed to progressFn while the tool runs,
102		// and kept so a failure can be reported with the tool's own diagnostic.
103		var stderr bytes.Buffer
104		if progressFn != nil {
105			pipe, err := cmd.StderrPipe()
106			if err == nil {
107				done := make(chan struct{})
108				go func() {
109					defer close(done)
110					sc := bufio.NewScanner(pipe)
111					for sc.Scan() {
112						line := strings.TrimSpace(sc.Text())
113						if line == "" {
114							continue
115						}
116						stderr.WriteString(line)
117						stderr.WriteByte('\n')
118						progressFn(line)
119					}
120					// A read failure on the progress pipe is not a scan failure:
121					// the report comes back on stdout, and the tool's exit code
122					// says whether it succeeded. Dropping the rest of the progress
123					// is the whole consequence.
124					_ = sc.Err()
125				}()
126				if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
127					return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s failed to start: %w", tc.Name, err)
128				}
129				<-done // drain stderr before Wait closes the pipe
130				return finish(tc.Name, cmd, &stdout, &stderr)
131			}
132		}
133	
134		cmd.Stderr = &stderr
135		if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
136			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s failed to start: %w", tc.Name, err)
137		}
138		return finish(tc.Name, cmd, &stdout, &stderr)
139	}
140	
141	// finish waits for the tool and only then reads what it wrote.
142	//
143	// The order is the point, and it is not a style preference: os/exec fills the
144	// output buffers from goroutines it owns, and only Wait guarantees they are
145	// done. Reading the buffer in the same expression as Wait — which is what
146	// `return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(..., cmd.Wait(), ...)` does, since operands
147	// are evaluated before the call — snapshots it while it is still empty, and
148	// every scan comes back with no findings.
149	func finish(name string, cmd *exec.Cmd, stdout, stderr *bytes.Buffer) ([]byte, error) {
150		err := cmd.Wait()
151		return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(name, err, stderr.String())
152	}
153	
154	// waitErr turns a non-zero exit into an *exitError carrying the code, and
155	// leaves anything else (a killed process, a broken pipe) as it is.
156	func waitErr(name string, err error, stderr string) error {
157		if err == nil {
158			return nil
159		}
160		var exitErr *exec.ExitError
161		if errors.As(err, &exitErr) {
162			if stderr == "" {
163				stderr = string(exitErr.Stderr)
164			}
165			return &exitError{Code: exitErr.ExitCode(), Stderr: stderr}
166		}
167		return fmt.Errorf("%s failed: %w", name, err)
168	}
169	
170	// runner is swapped by tests. Production code never reassigns it, so the
171	// package stays safe to call concurrently; tests that swap it must not run in
172	// parallel.
173	var runner commandRunner = cliRunner{}

16	// so one scan can be given a different answer for each stage it runs, and the
17	// calls are recorded so a test can say which tool was asked what.
18	//
19	// It is locked because Scanner.Scan runs its stages concurrently.
20	type scriptedRunner struct {
21		mu       sync.Mutex
22		calls    []toolCmd
23		progress []string
24		reply    func(toolCmd) ([]byte, error)
25	}
26	
27	func (r *scriptedRunner) Run(_ context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]byte, error) {
28		r.mu.Lock()
29		r.calls = append(r.calls, tc)
30		lines := r.progress
31		r.mu.Unlock()
32	
33		if progressFn != nil {
34			for _, line := range lines {
35				progressFn(line)
36			}
37		}
38		return r.reply(tc)
39	}
40	
41	func (r *scriptedRunner) commands() []string {
42		r.mu.Lock()
43		defer r.mu.Unlock()
44		out := make([]string, 0, len(r.calls))
45		for _, c := range r.calls {
46			out = append(out, c.String())
47		}
48		return out
49	}
50	
51	// commandForStage returns the invocation of one stage, or "" if it never ran.
52	//
53	// Scan runs its stages concurrently, so calls are recorded in completion order:
54	// a test that wants one scanner's command has to name the stage. Taking the
55	// last command that merely looked like Trivy is how this went: two stages
56	// invoke Trivy, and whichever finished second won.
57	func (r *scriptedRunner) commandForStage(stage string) string {
58		r.mu.Lock()
59		defer r.mu.Unlock()
60		for _, c := range r.calls {
61			if stageOf(c) == stage {
62				return c.String()
63			}
64		}
65		return ""
66	}
67	
68	func (r *scriptedRunner) count() int {
69		r.mu.Lock()
70		defer r.mu.Unlock()
71		return len(r.calls)
72	}

76	func useRunner(t *testing.T, r commandRunner) {
77		t.Helper()
78		previous := runner
79		runner = r
80		t.Cleanup(func() { runner = previous })

84	func answering(t *testing.T, stdout string, err error) *scriptedRunner {
85		t.Helper()

Oui, c'est voulu : le tableau `:templates` (`internal/ui/templates/model.go:126`, fonction `columns()`) n'affiche que les métadonnées du catalogue — icône, Name, Tags, Source, Ref. Aucune colonne de résultat de scan (Scanned, C/H/M/L, CI).

La raison (documentée dans `docs/architecture/templates.md`) : `S` sur un template écrit son contenu dans `~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>` et le fait scanner comme un **répertoire ordinaire**, mis en cache par chemin — le même mécanisme que pour les workspaces (`cache.StoreWorkspaceScan`). Le résultat apparaît donc dans l'inventaire **`:sec`**, pas dans `:templates` — « rien de nouveau à construire », et « la liste des workspaces n'est pas concernée : la copie n'y est pas, et rien ne prétend le contraire » s'applique symétriquement à `:templates`.

La colonne CI en particulier n'existe même pas conceptuellement ici : « No CI score. A template has no pipeline to grade, and plumber would look for a remote it does not have. »

Donc pour voir l'état de ton scan `go-http-api` : va dans `:sec`, il devrait y figurer comme une entrée scannée. `V` dans `:templates` ouvre juste un aperçu des fichiers, pas le résultat du scan.

content.text:
Non — plumber ne tournera **jamais** sur un scan de template, même si le template contient un `.github/workflows/ci.yml` ou un `.gitlab-ci.yml`.

C'est une désactivation explicite, pas une conséquence indirecte : `internal/ui/templates/scan.go:159-166` (`scanOptions()`) force `opts.EnableCIScore = false` avant de lancer le scan, peu importe la config globale de l'utilisateur. Le commentaire du code le dit : « a template is not a repository with a pipeline to grade, and plumber would go looking for a remote it does not have. »

Deux raisons de fond :
1. **Pas de remote à interroger** — `plumber analyze` prend son projet via `--project` auto-détecté depuis le remote git, ou explicitement fourni. Le répertoire matérialisé (`template.Materialize`) est un simple arbre de fichiers extrait via `git archive` — pas de `.git`, donc pas de remote.
2. **Pas de pipeline réel à noter** — même si le fichier CI existe dans les fichiers du template, il n'a jamais tourné sur ce repo précis (pas de repo GitHub/GitLab réel derrière), donc un score plumber n'aurait aucun sens à évaluer.

Donc un fichier CI dans ton `java/spring-boot` ou `go/http-api` restera invisible pour plumber tant qu'il vit dans le repo de templates. Il ne sera analysé qu'une fois le template appliqué et le repo réel créé sur le forge — via un scan normal de ce nouveau repo (`:sec` ou `ws`), qui lui aura un vrai remote.

1	package templates
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"strings"
6	
7		"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/textinput"
8		tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"
9		"github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss"
10	
11		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/template"
12		sharedcomponents "github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/components"
13		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/theme"
14	)
15	
16	// formField names one control of the form. The fields on screen depend on the
17	// source's kind, so focus is an index into fields(), not one of these.
18	type formField int
19	
20	const (
21		fieldName formField = iota
22		fieldDescription
23		fieldTags
24		fieldKind
25		fieldURL
26		fieldPath
27		fieldRef
28		fieldSubmit
29	)
30	
31	const (
32		descriptionWrapWidth = 80
33		descriptionCharLimit = 250
34	)
35	
36	// entryForm creates or edits a catalog entry. It is shown in the viewport, not
37	// as a modal (Rule 112).
38	type entryForm struct {
39		name, tags, url, path, ref textinput.Model
40		description                sharedcomponents.WrappedInput
41	
42		kind  int // index into template.Kinds
43		focus int // index into fields()
44	
45		// editing fixes the slug. Creating derives it from the name, so renaming a
46		// template does not silently orphan whatever remembered its old slug.
47		editing bool
48		slug    string
49		// taken reports whether a slug already names a declared entry.
50		taken func(slug string) bool
51	
52		err   string
53		width int
54	}
55	
56	// newEntryForm opens the form empty, or prefilled from an entry to edit it.
57	func newEntryForm(entry *template.Entry, taken func(string) bool) *entryForm {
58		f := &entryForm{
59			name:        newInput("Spring Boot API", 100),
60			tags:        newInput("java, spring-boot", 200),
61			url:         newInput("", 300),
62			path:        newInput("", 300),
63			ref:         newInput("", 100),
64			description: sharedcomponents.NewWrappedInput(descriptionWrapWidth, descriptionCharLimit, "description (optional)"),
65			taken:       taken,
66		}
67	
68		if entry != nil {
69			f.editing = true
70			f.slug = entry.Slug
71			f.name.SetValue(entry.Name)
72			f.description.SetValue(entry.Description)
73			f.tags.SetValue(strings.Join(entry.Tags, ", "))
74			f.url.SetValue(entry.Source.URL)
75			f.path.SetValue(entry.Source.Path)
76			f.ref.SetValue(entry.Source.Ref)
77			for i, k := range template.Kinds {
78				if k == entry.Source.Kind {
79					f.kind = i
80				}
81			}
82		}
83	
84		f.updateFocus()
85		return f
86	}
87	
88	func newInput(placeholder string, limit int) textinput.Model {
89		in := textinput.New()
90		in.Placeholder = placeholder
91		in.CharLimit = limit
92		in.Width = 60
93		theme.StyleTextInput(&in)
94		return in
95	}
96	
97	// SetWidth is called from the window-size handler.
98	func (f *entryForm) SetWidth(width int) {
99		f.width = width
100		f.description.SetDisplayWidth(width)
101	}
102	
103	func (f *entryForm) currentKind() template.Kind { return template.Kinds[f.kind] }
104	
105	// fields lists what is on screen, in order. A local template has no URL, so the
106	// field is absent rather than disabled: it is not that it cannot be filled, it
107	// is that it means nothing.
108	func (f *entryForm) fields() []formField {
109		list := []formField{fieldName, fieldDescription, fieldTags, fieldKind}
110		if f.currentKind() != template.KindLocal {
111			list = append(list, fieldURL)
112		}
113		return append(list, fieldPath, fieldRef, fieldSubmit)
114	}
115	
116	func (f *entryForm) focused() formField { return f.fields()[f.focus] }
117	
118	// Cycling is only meaningful on the kind field; the header greys ←→ elsewhere.
119	func (f *entryForm) OnCycleField() bool { return f.focused() == fieldKind }
120	
121	func (f *entryForm) updateFocus() {
122		f.name.Blur()
123		f.tags.Blur()
124		f.url.Blur()
125		f.path.Blur()
126		f.ref.Blur()
127		f.description.Blur()
128	
129		switch f.focused() {
130		case fieldName:
131			f.name.Focus()
132		case fieldDescription:
133			f.description.Focus()
134		case fieldTags:
135			f.tags.Focus()
136		case fieldURL:
137			f.url.Focus()
138		case fieldPath:
139			f.path.Focus()
140		case fieldRef:
141			f.ref.Focus()
142		}
143	}
144	
145	// InEditMode is always true while the form is open: `:` is a character in a URL.
146	func (f *entryForm) InEditMode() bool { return true }
147	
148	// Update handles a key. Keys follow Rule 135: ↑↓ move between fields, ←→ cycle
149	// the kind, tab does nothing, enter advances or confirms.
150	func (f *entryForm) Update(msg tea.KeyMsg) tea.Cmd {
151		switch msg.String() {
152		case "esc":
153			return func() tea.Msg { return FormCancelMsg{} }
154	
155		case "down":
156			f.move(1)
157			return nil
158	
159		case "up":
160			f.move(-1)
161			return nil
162	
163		case "tab", "shift+tab":
164			return nil
165	
166		case "enter":
167			if f.focused() == fieldSubmit {
168				return f.submit()
169			}
170			f.move(1)
171			return nil
172	
173		case "left", "right":
174			if f.focused() == fieldKind {
175				f.cycleKind(msg.String() == "right")
176				return nil
177			}
178		}
179	
180		return f.forward(msg)
181	}
182	
183	func (f *entryForm) move(delta int) {
184		n := len(f.fields())
185		f.focus = (f.focus + delta + n) % n
186		f.updateFocus()
187	}
188	
189	// cycleKind moves to the next or previous kind. The focus stays on the kind
190	// field, which sits above every field that changes.
191	func (f *entryForm) cycleKind(forward bool) {
192		n := len(template.Kinds)
193		if forward {
194			f.kind = (f.kind + 1) % n
195		} else {
196			f.kind = (f.kind - 1 + n) % n
197		}
198		f.err = ""
199	}
200	
201	func (f *entryForm) forward(msg tea.KeyMsg) tea.Cmd {
202		var cmd tea.Cmd
203		switch f.focused() {
204		case fieldName:
205			f.name, cmd = f.name.Update(msg)
206		case fieldDescription:
207			f.description, cmd = f.description.Update(msg)
208		case fieldTags:
209			f.tags, cmd = f.tags.Update(msg)
210		case fieldURL:
211			f.url, cmd = f.url.Update(msg)
212		case fieldPath:
213			f.path, cmd = f.path.Update(msg)
214		case fieldRef:
215			f.ref, cmd = f.ref.Update(msg)
216		}
217		return cmd
218	}
219	
220	// entry is what the form currently describes.
221	func (f *entryForm) entry() (template.Entry, error) {
222		slug := f.slug
223		if !f.editing {
224			slug = slugify(f.name.Value())
225		}
226	
227		src := template.Source{Kind: f.currentKind(), Path: strings.TrimSpace(f.path.Value()), Ref: strings.TrimSpace(f.ref.Value())}
228		if src.Kind != template.KindLocal {
229			src.URL = strings.TrimSpace(f.url.Value())
230		}
231	
232		e := template.Entry{
233			Slug:        slug,
234			Name:        strings.TrimSpace(f.name.Value()),
235			Description: strings.TrimSpace(f.description.Value()),
236			Tags:        template.NormalizeTags(strings.Split(f.tags.Value(), ",")),
237			Source:      src,
238		}
239		if slug == "" {
240			return e, fmt.Errorf("the name needs a letter or a digit")
241		}
242		if !f.editing && f.taken != nil && f.taken(slug) {
243			return e, fmt.Errorf("a template named %q already exists", slug)
244		}
245		return e, e.Validate()
246	}
247	
248	// submit validates in place: an invalid entry keeps the form open with the
249	// reason, rather than sending a message the view would only turn back.
250	func (f *entryForm) submit() tea.Cmd {
251		e, err := f.entry()
252		if err != nil {
253			f.err = err.Error()
254			return nil
255		}
256		f.err = ""
257		return func() tea.Msg { return FormSubmitMsg{Entry: e} }
258	}
259	
260	// slugify makes the identifier of a new entry from its name.
261	func slugify(name string) string {
262		var b strings.Builder
263		dash := false
264		for _, r := range strings.ToLower(name) {
265			switch {
266			case r >= 'a' && r <= 'z', r >= '0' && r <= '9':
267				if dash && b.Len() > 0 {
268					b.WriteByte('-')
269				}
270				dash = false
271				b.WriteRune(r)
272			default:
273				dash = true
274			}
275		}
276		return b.String()
277	}
278	
279	// GetTitle is the form's breadcrumb.
280	func (f *entryForm) GetTitle() string {
281		if f.editing {
282			return "Edit template"
283		}
284		return "New template"
285	}
286	
287	// View renders the form: one blank line of top padding (Rule 131), then the
288	// fields with the focus marker (Rule 120).
289	func (f *entryForm) View() string {
290		var b strings.Builder
291		b.WriteString(theme.EmptyLineBg(f.width) + "\n")
292	
293		if f.err != "" {
294			b.WriteString(lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground).Foreground(theme.ColorError).Render("Error: "+f.err) + "\n\n")
295		}
296	
297		labels := f.labels()
298		for _, field := range f.fields() {
299			switch field {
300			case fieldName:
301				b.WriteString(f.line(field, "Name", f.name.View()) + "\n")
302			case fieldDescription:
303				b.WriteString(f.descriptionBlock() + "\n\n")
304			case fieldTags:
305				b.WriteString(f.line(field, "Tags", f.tags.View()) + "\n")
306			case fieldKind:
307				b.WriteString(f.kindLine() + "\n")
308			case fieldURL:
309				b.WriteString(f.line(field, labels.url, f.url.View()) + "\n")
310			case fieldPath:
311				b.WriteString(f.line(field, labels.path, f.path.View()) + "\n")
312			case fieldRef:
313				b.WriteString(f.line(field, labels.ref, f.ref.View()) + "\n")
314			case fieldSubmit:
315				label := "Create"
316				if f.editing {
317					label = "Save"
318				}
319				b.WriteString("\n  " + theme.RenderButton(label, true, "primary") + "\n")
320			}
321		}
322		return b.String()
323	}
324	
325	// kindLabels names the three source fields for the kind on screen. The same
326	// three inputs serve every kind — a value typed before cycling the kind is kept
327	// — and only what they are called changes.
328	type kindLabels struct{ url, path, ref string }
329	
330	func (f *entryForm) labels() kindLabels {
331		switch f.currentKind() {
332		case template.KindLocal:
333			return kindLabels{path: "Directory", ref: "Branch, tag or SHA"}
334		case template.KindOCI:
335			return kindLabels{url: "Registry URL", path: "Repository", ref: "Tag"}
336		default:
337			return kindLabels{url: "Clone URL", path: "Subdirectory", ref: "Branch, tag or SHA"}
338		}
339	}
340	
341	// line renders a single-line field: label and value on the same line (Rule 113).
342	func (f *entryForm) line(field formField, label, value string) string {
343		if f.focused() == field {
344			return theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall+" "+label+" "+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
345		}
346		return theme.Bg("  "+label+" "+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
347	}
348	
349	// kindLine is the ←→ cycle field (Rule 132).
350	func (f *entryForm) kindLine() string {
351		label := "Source " + theme.IconSelect + " "
352		value := lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground).Foreground(theme.ColorText).Render(string(f.currentKind()))
353		if f.focused() == fieldKind {
354			return theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall+" "+label+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
355		}
356		return theme.Bg("  "+label+theme.IconChevronRight+" ") + value
357	}
358	
359	// descriptionBlock is the multi-line field: label, then the wrapped input.
360	func (f *entryForm) descriptionBlock() string {
361		label := theme.Bg("  Description " + theme.IconChevronRight)
362		if f.focused() == fieldDescription {
363			label = theme.KeyStyle.Render(theme.IconCircleSmall + " Description " + theme.IconChevronRight)
364		}
365		return label + "\n" + f.description.View()
366	}

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **AI Collaboration Rule**:
> - **Planning**, **Brainstorming**, **Implementation** and **Bug fixes** are all
>   in scope. Planning is no longer delegated to Gemini (Antigravity).
> - Implementation plans go in `.claude/plans/` (see
>   [rules/planning.md](rules/planning.md)); design decisions that outlive a plan
>   are recorded in `docs/backlog.md`.
> - Always refer to [project-context.md](../project-context.md) for global project rules.
>   It sits in this repository, at the root. The absolute path this line used to
>   carry named a GitLab checkout that is no longer where DevDesk lives.

## Project Overview

DevDesk is a terminal-based TUI (Text User Interface) application built with Go and Bubble Tea framework. It provides DevSecOps functionality including:
- System status monitoring (HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP, DNS, SSL checks)
- GitLab integration (authentication, project explorer, multi-select clone)
- Security scanning (Trivy CVE/secret/license/misconfig + Gitleaks secrets)
- Container management with real-time metrics, on Docker or Podman (`app.container_engine`)
- OCI resource management (image scanning, container launching, network inspection)
- Network diagnostics (DNS, route, ICMP, TCP, TLS, HTTP) + real-time port monitoring + this machine's interfaces
- Multi-context configuration management via YAML
- Local workspaces management with git metadata

## Build and Development Commands

Tasks live in `mise.toml` — there is no Makefile. `mise tasks` lists them all.

```bash
# Development (fastest)
mise run dev          # Run directly with go run
go run .

# Build
mise run build        # Build binary to bin/dk
mise run run          # Build and run

# Testing
mise run test         # Run all tests
mise run cover        # Coverage per package
go test -v ./...      # Run all tests with verbose output
go test ./internal/command  # Run tests for specific package
mise run test-race    # Detect race conditions (critical for Bubble Tea Cmds)

# Code Quality
mise run fmt          # Format code
mise run vet          # Run go vet
mise run lint         # MANDATORY before commits - golangci-lint
mise run tidy         # Tidy dependencies
mise run check        # fmt + vet + lint + test in one go

# Installation
mise run install      # Install to $GOPATH/bin
```

`test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler (`gcc`/`clang`) on `PATH`.

## Work starts in a new worktree

**Any task that will produce a commit begins with its own worktree**, cut from
the current `main`, **under `.worktrees/` inside the repository**:

```bash
git fetch origin main
git worktree add -b <branch> .worktrees/<branch> origin/main
cd .worktrees/<branch>
```

Answering a question, reading code, running the app — none of that needs one.
Editing does.

**Under the repository, not beside it.** This reverses what this file said until
now, and the reason it gave was wrong. It claimed a worktree at `.worktrees/x`
would be compiled by `go build ./...` and `go test ./...`. It would not: the go
tool skips every directory whose name begins with `.` or `_`, so `.worktrees/`
is invisible to `./...`. Verified rather than assumed — a package of deliberately
invalid Go placed under `.worktrees/` builds clean and `go list ./...` does not
name it. The old argument holds for `worktrees/` without the dot, which is
presumably where it came from.

What decides it is the **sandbox mount**, and it cost a full debugging session to
find. A direct-mode sandbox mounts *this directory only*. A sibling worktree at
`../devdesk-<branch>` is therefore outside the mount, so its **files** are written
into the container's private layer and never reach the host — while `.git` is
inside the mount and stays shared. Refs agree, files diverge, and nothing warns:
the branch tip moves, the host's copy of those files does not, and `git status`
on the host reports the *stale* content as uncommitted modifications. An agent
and the person testing its work end up compiling different code while both
believe they are on the same branch. Under `.worktrees/`, host and sandbox see
one filesystem.

Two effects worth knowing, neither blocking:

- `.worktrees/` is in `.gitignore`; a worktree there is not a change to the tree.
- Claude Code discovers the nested `.claude/` of each worktree, so its skills and
  rules appear a second time, prefixed by the worktree path. Harmless, and the
  price of the directory being inside the repo.

**What isolates, and what does not.** git refuses to check out one branch in two
worktrees, so two agents cannot land on the same branch by accident — that is the
whole protection, and it is worth knowing what it does *not* cover:

| Shared by every worktree | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `~/.devdesk/` — contexts, `config.yaml`, scan caches | two agents editing settings or scanning at once overwrite each other's; nothing warns |
| the host keyring, Docker, the ports the app binds | one at a time, whoever gets there first |
| `.git/hooks` | verified: `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` resolves to the **main** checkout's, so the Entire checkpoint and pre-push hooks fire normally from a worktree |
| `origin` | inherited — `git push -u origin <branch>` goes through the mirror as usual |

`mise` tasks and `go build` work unchanged; both read the tree they are run in.

**`entire graph` indexes per directory.** A fresh worktree has no index, so the
first `entire graph search` there pays a full build (~5 s on this repo, measured)
and the symbol ids it returns are namespaced by the directory name
(`local/<branch>:Go:…`). Nothing breaks; do not be surprised by the first search
being slow or by ids that do not match another worktree's.

**Clean up when the PR is merged**, from the main checkout:

```bash
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
git worktree list          # what is still out there
git worktree prune         # after a directory was deleted by hand
```

`git worktree remove` refuses a tree with uncommitted changes, which is the
point — look before forcing.

**The main checkout stays on `main` and stays clean.** It is what `git fetch
origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main` needs after each merge, and what
every new worktree is cut from.

## Git workflow — pull requests only

**Never push directly to `main`.** The Entire mirror rejects it:

```
! [remote rejected] main -> main (protected branch)
```

This is enforced by the mirror, not by GitHub, and **Entire does not document it**
— neither the CLI help nor `docs.entire.io` mentions a protected default branch.
The only branch restriction Entire states is that `entire/unmirrored/*` is never
forwarded. Treat the rejection as observed behaviour, not as a specified one.

**The repository is public since 2026-09-06**, which is what makes GitHub-side
enforcement possible at all: a private repo on a free personal plan answers
`403 Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public` on both
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/branches/main/protection` and
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/rulesets` — that was the prior state, and it is not a
description to trust going forward if the repo ever goes private again. Do not
cite `gh api repos/anthnel/devdesk/branches/main` reporting `"protected":
false` as proof of anything either way: that field only ever reflects legacy
branch protection, so it reads `false` under a ruleset too, and it read `false`
on the free-private plan whatever the configuration. Query
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/rulesets` itself (or `gh ruleset check main`) for the
real answer.

A ruleset named `main-protection` (id `22399372`) now targets `refs/heads/main`
only — deliberately not `entire/checkpoints/v1`, which receives automatic
pushes from the Entire hook and would break if rule-gated. It requires a pull
request (0 approving reviews — solo maintainer, the PR is a record not a review
gate) with the `Lint and build` and `Test` checks from `ci.yml` passing,
blocks force-pushes and branch deletion, and grants no bypass. This closes the
gap the mirror alone left open: the Entire mirror's rejection of a direct push
to `main` was, until now, the *only* protection — a second remote pointing
straight at GitHub would have sailed through (see the warning against adding
one, below). Now GitHub itself refuses that push too.

Every other branch, including `entire/checkpoints/v1`, pushes through the mirror
and is forwarded to GitHub.

**Pull requests are GitHub's, not Entire's.** Entire has no merge-request
concept — it layers checkpoints and sessions over git and forwards pushes. So
the PR steps below are `gh`, and the branch they review is one `origin` carried
to GitHub. `entire review` (labs) runs a multi-agent review against the current
branch and is a pre-merge step, not a substitute for the PR.

```bash
git worktree add -b <branch> .worktrees/<branch> origin/main   # work happens here
git push -u origin <branch>                     # via the mirror — forwarded to GitHub
gh pr create -R anthnel/devdesk --base main --head <branch>
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash --delete-branch
# then, from the main checkout:
git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main   # may need a retry, see below
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
```

**`-R anthnel/devdesk` is not optional.** `gh` infers the repository from a
remote pointing at a GitHub host, and `origin` is an `entire://` URL, so it
finds none and fails with *"none of the git remotes configured for this
repository point to a known GitHub host"*. The flag names the repo directly.
Do not solve this by adding a GitHub remote — see below.

**After a merge, `origin` can read stale for a minute or two.** The mirror lags
GitHub, so `git fetch origin` right after `gh pr merge` may return the *previous*
`main` — with no error, which is the part that misleads. `gh pr view <n> --json state`
says `MERGED` while `git rev-parse origin/main` still points at the commit before
it. Re-run the fetch a moment later; `gh` is what to trust in the meantime,
because it talks to GitHub directly and needs no remote.

**Do not add a second remote pointing at GitHub to work around that.** The
`main-protection` ruleset (above) would now refuse a direct `git push github
main` too, so it is no longer the *only* defeat of the only protection — but a
direct push still bypasses the mirror, and with it the Entire hook that
records checkpoints and sessions, which is not visible until much later.
`origin` is the only remote, deliberately.

**Merging several branches cut from the same commit conflicts in
`docs/backlog.md`.** Every fix inserts its entry at the top of §1.1, so the
second and third merges land on the same anchor. The resolution is always to
keep both sides — they are independent entries, not competing edits.

### Landing a sandbox-made commit (host-relay)

A Docker Sandbox (`sbx`) has no `entire://` auth of its own — `ENTIRE_TOKEN`
via `sbx secret set-custom` doesn't work (`git-remote-entire` parses the
JWT's claims locally, before any network call, but the secret proxy only
substitutes the real token on the wire — the sandbox process itself only
ever sees an unparseable placeholder), and an interactive `entire login`
inside the sandbox trades that for a persistent, harder-to-reason-about
credential sitting in a less-trusted place. So the sandbox edits and commits
locally only; the host does every `origin` operation — fetch, push, PR,
merge. `git pull`/`git fetch` run *inside* the sandbox will fail with `no
auth context for cluster ...` — that's expected, not a setup bug; don't
`entire login` there to fix it (see `~/projects/github/anthnel/sbx-kits/entire/README.md`
for the full rationale).

A direct-mode sandbox mounts this exact repo directory, so both the commits and
the working files land where the host sees them — provided the worktree is under
`.worktrees/`, which is why that is the rule. There is nothing to transfer; the
host only has to push, because the sandbox has no `entire://` auth:

```bash
# From the host, once the sandbox reports "done and committed":
git push origin <branch>
gh pr create -R anthnel/devdesk --base main --head <branch> --fill
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash --delete-branch
git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main   # may need a retry, see above
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
```

**If a worktree was made at the old sibling path** (`../devdesk-<branch>`), the
host cannot see its files and `git worktree list` shows it `prunable`. The
commits are still in the shared `.git/objects`, so nothing is lost — but the
host's copy of those files is stale, and `git status` there reports that stale
content as uncommitted modifications, which reads as if work were pending when
the opposite is true. Recover by taking the branch tip:

```bash
git stash push -m "stale files from a sandbox sibling worktree"   # reversible
git worktree prune -v                  # drop the unreachable admin entry
git push origin <sha>:refs/heads/<branch>
```

**A worktree created from inside the sandbox registers a Linux path the
host's git can't resolve — even under `.worktrees/`.** `.worktrees/` shares
*files* between host and sandbox, but each side's git still writes its own
`.git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir` pointer, and the sandbox's git records a Linux
path (`/c/Users/...`). The host's `git worktree remove` on that same
directory then fails with `fatal: '<path>' is not a working tree` — Windows
git cannot resolve the pointer left behind. The costlier part: a plain `git
worktree prune` run on the host right after that failure deregisters the
worktree **silently** — git treats an unresolvable pointer as a worktree
that's gone — while leaving alone any sibling worktree whose path it *can*
read. If the branch was already merged the content is safe either way, but a
host-run `prune` while an agent is still working inside a sandbox-created
worktree would deregister that worktree out from under it, mid-task, with
nothing on either side raising a warning. The rule this implies: **whoever
creates a worktree removes it** — do not `git worktree remove` or `prune`
from the other side of the host/sandbox split.

#### Developing in the sandbox, testing from the host

This is the normal mode, and the split works out well: **git is what the
host does not need in the worktree, the build is what the sandbox does not
need.** Measured in a worktree whose pointer carries a Linux path, from the
host:

| From the host, in `.worktrees/<branch>/` | Result |
|---|---|
| any `git` command | `fatal: not a git repository: (NULL)` |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go test ./internal/command/` | `ok … 0.239s` |
| `go build .` (with buildvcs stamping) | exit 0 |
| `mise run build` | OK |

The breakage is therefore **entirely** on the git side, not just on
`worktree remove`: Go does not need the VCS, and `-buildvcs=auto` degrades
silently rather than failing when it gets no answer. The main checkout is
never affected.

The resulting split of responsibilities:

1. **The sandbox creates the worktree** — it is the one that will commit
   into it, so it is the one that must keep a working git.
2. **The sandbox edits and commits.** All the git activity happens there.
3. **The host builds, tests, and runs the application** in that same
   directory, since the files are shared through the mount. No git command
   here — the `fatal` above is expected, it does not signal a broken repo.
4. **To read the diff from the host, go through the main checkout**: the
   refs and `.git/objects` are shared, so it sees everything the sandbox
   committed — `git log --oneline main..<branch>`, `git diff main...<branch>`.
5. **The host pushes and merges from the main checkout**, never from the
   worktree — that is the host-relay above.
6. **The sandbox removes its worktree.** If it no longer exists, the host can
   delete the *files* (they are inside the mount, unlike the sibling case
   above) then `git worktree prune` — but only once no sandbox still has a
   live worktree.

**Testing from the host is not a workaround.** DevDesk needs a real
terminal, the host's Docker socket, the host's secret manager
(`internal/credentials`), `~/.devdesk/`, and binding ports: none of that is
representative inside the sandbox. What the sandbox does better is write
code.

**The reverse direction is forbidden**: the host does not create the
worktree for the sandbox to work in. By symmetry, the `C:/Users/...` path
Windows git writes is not resolvable under Linux — the sandbox would lose
the git it needs to commit. (This direction has not been tested; it is the
same mechanism read backwards.)

**A follow-up commit on the same branch, after the first one already got
squash-merged, will conflict on a plain `git merge`** — squashing rewrites
history, so `git merge origin/main` computes the wrong common ancestor
(the branch's *own* pre-squash parent) and re-diffs files that already
landed, even when nothing actually conflicts in substance. Don't hand-edit
through that; cherry-pick the new commit straight onto current `origin/main`
instead — its real parent already matches what's on `main`, so it applies
clean:

```bash
git worktree add -b <tmp-branch> .worktrees/<tmp-branch> <new-sha>
cd .worktrees/<tmp-branch>
git reset --hard origin/main
git cherry-pick <new-sha>              # clean apply — verify before trusting this
go build ./... && go test ./<touched-packages>/...
git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch-name>
# gh pr create / gh pr merge as above, then from the main checkout:
git worktree remove .worktrees/<tmp-branch>
```

### Publishing a release — release-please, then goreleaser

**A release takes two merges, and that is the point.** `release-please`
watches `main` and keeps a **release pull request** open: it reads the
conventional commits since the last tag, decides the version, and writes
`CHANGELOG.md`. Merging that PR creates the tag and the GitHub Release;
`goreleaser` then builds the six binaries (linux, darwin, windows × amd64,
arm64) and attaches them to that Release.

#### The flow, plainly — accumulate, then release whenever you want

The two actors: `release-please` **proposes** (it never writes directly to
`main` except through its own PR), `goreleaser` **builds**, and it only
triggers once that PR is merged. Concrete timeline:

1. A `fix:` or a `feat:` is merged onto `main` (a normal work PR, see
   above). The code ships right away. release-please sees that commit and
   **creates or updates** — never two PRs in parallel — the
   "chore(main): release x.y.z" PR with the corresponding changelog; that PR
   only touches `CHANGELOG.md` and `.release-please-manifest.json`.
2. Step 1 repeats as many times as wanted — several fixes, one or several
   features, over days or weeks. Each merge grows the same release PR (the
   version number can climb, a `feat:` bumps the minor) without any tag
   being set and without any binary being published.
3. When the moment is judged right — and only then — the release PR itself
   gets merged. That specific merge, and only that one, sets the tag,
   creates the GitHub Release, and wakes up goreleaser.

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| Merge a `fix:`/`feat:` onto `main` | Code shipped immediately; the release PR updates in the background; nothing is published |
| Merge the release PR | **Sole trigger for publishing** — tag, Release, binaries |

Publishing is therefore never a per-commit act: it is a deliberate act,
decided by merging a PR that already exists and that can be left to grow
indefinitely.

```bash
# nothing to run: the release PR opens and updates itself on its own
gh pr list -R anthnel/devdesk --label "autorelease: pending"
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash   # ← this merge is what publishes
```

**Why not semantic-release**, which would achieve the same thing in a single
merge: it pushes the tag directly to `main`, and this repository forbids
that — the Entire mirror rejects that push, and this refusal is the *only*
protection `main` has, since branch protection is unavailable on this plan
(the 403 above). One extra merge per release is the price of that rule.

**The mirror replicates tags, verified on 2026-09-06.** The tag is set by
GitHub Actions, so it is born on GitHub and not via the mirror — but
`git fetch origin --tags` brings it back, just as it brings back a
squash-merge done by `gh`. That was the only unknown in the chain, and it is
now resolved: nothing forces setting a tag by hand.

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `release-please-config.json` | the type (`go`), the CHANGELOG sections |
| `.release-please-manifest.json` | the current version — **written by the bot**, never by hand |
| `.goreleaser.yaml` | the six targets, the `-ldflags`, `mode: append` |
| `.github/workflows/release.yml` | the two jobs, chained by `release_created` |

**A repository setting no workflow can grant itself**: *Settings →
Actions → Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests*. Without
it, the first run fails on the PR it cannot open, and the message does not
say that is why. **Already active here** —
`gh api repos/anthnel/devdesk/actions/permissions/workflow` answers
`can_approve_pull_request_reviews: true`, verified on 2026-09-06. The same
call shows `default_workflow_permissions: read`, which is not a problem:
that is the default when a workflow states nothing, and `release.yml`
declares its own.

**The binary's version comes from `-ldflags`**, not from a committed file
(§3.62). `release-please` knows how to write into a Go file (`versionFile`)
and it is not used for that: it would be a second source of truth for an
answer the build already gives, and a dev binary would then show the number
of the last release instead of `dev`.

**Before pushing a change to the chain**, `mise run release-check` validates
the configuration and `mise run release-snapshot` builds the six targets
without publishing anything — it is the only way to discover a broken target
before a tag is set.

**The first release will list the whole history** (66 `feat:` and 50 `fix:`
as of 2026-09-06). This is deliberate — an empty first CHANGELOG would be
worse — and the PR is editable before the merge. To start at `1.0.0` rather
than `0.1.0`, a one-off `"release-as": "1.0.0"` in the config, removed
afterward.

### Remotes

| Remote | URL | Use |
|--------|-----|-----|
| `origin` | `entire://aws-eu-central-1.entire.io/gh/anthnel/devdesk` | Entire mirror — everything: clone, fetch, push |

**There is one remote, and there should stay one.** The repository is hosted on
GitHub and mirrored to EntireDB in `aws-eu-central-1` (a second placement exists
in `aws-us-east-2`), but every git operation goes through the mirror: it is the

goes through `gh`, which authenticates directly and does not need a remote.

Semantic search (`entire search`, and the `entire:*` skills that depend on it) is
**not available in the EU region** — the server answers `semantic search is not
yet available in the region(s) hosting this search`. Nothing in the repo config
fixes this.
